big: Two shares both trade at a P/E of 40. One grows earnings 40% a year, the other 8%. Same price tag, very different value. The P/E alone does not tell you which is dear.

lines: Is a high P/E always bad?

No. A high P/E can be fair when growth is high and lasts. It is dangerous when growth slows. Compare with PEG, which is P/E divided by growth. Compare earnings yield, 1 ÷ P/E, with the 10-year G-sec yield. And market cap to GDP gives a rough read on the overall market.

q: A share has a P/E of 40 and earnings growth of 40%. What is its PEG?
why: 80 adds the two instead of dividing.

q: What does the earnings yield of a stock at P/E 40 equal?
why: 40% mixes up P/E with a yield.
4% is not one over forty, no.
25% is one over four, not forty.

q: When is a high P/E more acceptable?
opts: When growth is high and durable
When the company posts a loss
why: High, lasting growth can support it.

q: What does market cap to GDP give?
opts: A guaranteed signal of a fall
The exact price of one single share
A rough read on market valuation
The dividend paid by each company
why: It is not a single-stock price.
It is a broad, rough gauge.
It is not a dividend measure.

pts: P/E = price ÷ EPS. PEG = P/E ÷ growth.
Earnings yield = 1 ÷ P/E, compared with the G-sec yield.
High P/E is fine with durable growth, risky if growth slows.
